entries.narration: In the Docker course, running a container was a single command, and you were the one watching it. Now picture the same catalogue API running as several copies, spread across several machines, for months. Someone has to decide which machine each copy runs on. Someone has to notice when a machine disappears, and start the missing copy somewhere else. Clients need one stable name to reach, even though the copies behind it keep changing. And a new version has to replace the old one without taking the service down. That ongoing coordination is what an orchestrator takes over, and Kubernetes is one. But it is worth being precise about the boundary from the very start. Kubernetes keeps processes running; it has no idea whether they are correct. If the API returns the wrong price, Kubernetes will faithfully run two copies of that mistake. It does not keep your data consistent, it cannot place work on machines that do not exist, and it can only judge health through the signals your application chooses to expose. Every chapter in this course returns to that line between cluster automation and application correctness.

Here is the idea the rest of Kubernetes is built on. You do not issue a sequence of commands, like start this, then start that. You declare what should be true, and the system keeps working until it is true. Every object carries two halves. The spec is the desired state, and you write it: say, two replicas of the catalogue API. The status is the observed state, and the system writes it: right now, perhaps, one replica exists and one is ready. Notice that a gap between those two is completely normal. It is not an error; it is simply work that has not finished yet. Closing the gap is the job of a controller, and a controller runs the same small loop forever. It observes the current status, compares it with the spec, and acts to close the difference, here by creating one more Pod. Then it does it again. Because the loop never stops, the same mechanism handles your first deployment and a machine failure at three in the morning. The cost is that convergence is not instant, and it can only finish if the cluster has the capacity to make the spec true.

A Kubernetes cluster divides into two kinds of responsibility. The control plane decides; the worker nodes execute. The control plane holds every object you declare, and the history of changes to it. It decides which node each Pod should run on, and it runs the controllers that keep reconciling each kind of object. Your application containers do not run there. They run on worker nodes, and each node carries an agent called the kubelet. The kubelet watches for Pods assigned to its node, starts their containers through a container runtime, and reports back how those Pods, and the node itself, are doing. Keeping these apart matters in practice. A node that is overloaded by your application does not slow down the cluster's decision making. And if a node disappears, what is lost is running work, not your intent. The desired state is still stored in the control plane, so the controllers notice the shortfall and recreate the missing Pods on a node that remains. In a managed cluster, the control plane is often invisible to you entirely, which is exactly why it helps to know what it is doing.

Let's follow one change through the cluster, from your terminal to a running process. The first thing to notice is the shape. Every component talks to the API server, and none of them call each other directly. Instead, each one watches the API for the objects it is responsible for. So, step one: kubectl sends your manifest to the API server over HTTPS. Step two: the API server checks who you are, validates the object, and persists it in etcd, the cluster's datastore. Step three: a controller, watching for that kind of object, sees that two Pods are wanted and none exist, so it creates two Pod objects, again through the API. Step four: the scheduler sees Pods with no node assigned, and binds each one to a node with room for it. Step five: the kubelet on that node sees a Pod bound to it, and asks the container runtime to pull the image and start the process. Two practical consequences follow. When apply succeeds, your object has been stored, not started. And because every step is separate, each one can stall on its own, and each one leaves its own evidence in status and events.

Coming from the Docker course, it is natural to assume Kubernetes runs Docker underneath. It is cleaner than that. The image you built with Docker runs on Kubernetes unchanged, because what matters is the image format, not the tool that produced it. At build time, Docker, or any builder that produces OCI images, turns your Dockerfile into layers and configuration, and you push the result to a registry, addressed by a tag and, more precisely, by a digest. At run time, the kubelet on each node does not talk to Docker at all. It speaks a narrow interface called the Container Runtime Interface, or CRI, to a runtime such as containerd or CRI-O. That runtime pulls the image from the registry and starts the container as an isolated process. So a node does not need a Docker daemon, and the commands you used to inspect containers on your laptop are usually the wrong tool on a cluster. The practical rule is simple. Use build tools to debug the image you produce. Once it is running, inspect it through the Kubernetes API, where its status, events, and logs are recorded.

You will meet Kubernetes in three broad settings, and it helps to know which one you are in. A local cluster runs on one machine, often as a single node. It is ideal for learning, because you can break it and reset it freely, but it proves that something behaves correctly, not that it would stay available. A managed cluster is run by a provider. They operate the control plane, and often its upgrades, while you still choose node pools, decide when nodes are upgraded, and pay for what you use. Managed clusters also tend to come with integrated storage and load balancers. A self-managed cluster is the other extreme. You run every component yourself, including etcd and its backups, you choose the networking and storage plugins, and you are the one who gets paged. All three serve the same API, so everything in this course applies to each of them. And one thing never moves: your manifests, your images, your data, and who has access stay your responsibility everywhere. Throughout the course, record the versions you actually run, and remember that a demonstration on a laptop is not a claim about production.

Every kubectl command makes a decision before it sends anything: which cluster to talk to, which identity to present, and which namespace to work in. Those three answers live in a kubeconfig file. It lists clusters, meaning API server addresses and the certificates to trust; users, meaning the credentials to present; and contexts, which bundle one cluster, one user, and a default namespace under a single name. The current context is simply the bundle in use right now. This matters because Kubernetes will carry out a perfectly correct command in the wrong place without complaint. If your current context points at a shared cluster rather than your learning cluster, an apply or a delete goes there. Namespaces add a second layer. They scope names, so the same object name can exist in two namespaces, but on their own they are not a security boundary, and some objects, such as nodes, are cluster-scoped and belong to no namespace at all. So the habit for this whole course is simple. Check the current context before any change, and name the namespace explicitly, even when a default is already set.

Look at the first two lines of any manifest, because they decide how the rest is read. The apiVersion names a group and a version. For a Deployment that is apps slash v1: the apps group, version one. A handful of the oldest, core kinds, such as Pod and Service, have no group, so they just say v1. Then kind names the type itself. Together they tell the API server which schema to validate your fields against, and the server exposes that kind at a resource path, here deployments, which is what the URL and the permissions actually refer to. Versions are also promises. A stable v1 API keeps its fields; alpha and beta APIs can change shape or disappear between releases, which is why this course keeps its core examples on stable APIs, and why you should record the versions your cluster serves. Finally, do not trust memory, including mine, for exact fields. kubectl explain reads the schema the server actually serves, field by field, and kubectl api-resources lists which kinds this particular cluster supports, including any extensions it has installed.

When you read an object back from the API, it is larger than the manifest you sent, and the extra parts are where the evidence lives. Metadata is identity and bookkeeping. You supply the name, the namespace, and labels; the system adds a unique ID, a resource version, owner references, and more. Spec is the desired state you declared. Status is what the system has observed, and it is written by controllers, never by you; if you put a status block in your manifest, it is simply ignored. Three fields make that comparison precise. Generation goes up each time the spec changes. Observed generation, in the status, records which generation the controller has actually processed. And conditions describe the state in small structured records, each with a type, a true or false status, and a reason. So the reading is mechanical. If the observed generation matches the generation, and the conditions you care about are true, the object has converged. If the observed generation lags behind, the controller simply has not caught up yet. That distinction saves a lot of false alarms.

Kubernetes connects objects by query, not by name, and that is the idea to hold onto in this section. Start with identity. A name is unique for its kind within a namespace, and it can be reused: delete catalogue-api, create it again, and the name is the same. The UID is different. It is unique for all time, so a recreated object is, as far as the system is concerned, a brand new object. Labels are small key and value pairs you attach for grouping, such as app equals catalogue and tier equals api. A selector is a query over those labels. A Service or a Deployment does not keep a list of its Pods; it continuously selects whatever currently carries matching labels. On the left, the selector matches two of four Pods. The database is excluded by its tier label, as intended. The fourth Pod is excluded by a typo, catalog instead of catalogue, and nothing warns you. That one character is a common reason a Service has no endpoints. Annotations look similar but serve a different purpose: free-form notes for tools and people, never used for selection.

Declarative workflow means the manifest file is your record of intent, and the cluster is asked to make itself match it. The safe sequence has three steps before anything changes. Confirm the context and namespace. Ask the server to validate the change with a dry run, which runs it through the real schema and admission checks without storing it. Then read the diff, which shows exactly which fields would change on the live object. Only then apply. Behind the scenes, the server tracks who set each field, recording a field manager per field. That matters as soon as two writers share an object. Suppose you own the image and ports, and an autoscaler owns the replica count. If your manifest also sets replicas, server-side apply reports a conflict rather than silently overwriting the autoscaler's choice. You can force it, which takes ownership of the field, but that should be a deliberate decision, not a reflex. Be aware, too, that the older client-side apply tracks this differently, and that create, replace, and interactive edits skip the preview habit altogether.

Deleting one object can delete many, and owner references are how Kubernetes knows which. A Deployment owns its ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet owns its Pods. Each dependent carries an owner reference pointing at its owner. When an owner is deleted, a garbage collector finds dependents whose owner has gone and removes them too. That cascade is the default, but you can ask for foreground deletion, where dependents go first, or orphan the dependents and leave them running. Finalizers add a pause to this. A finalizer is a named promise on an object that some cleanup must finish before it disappears. When you delete such an object, it does not vanish; it gains a deletion timestamp and waits until every finalizer has been removed by whoever owns that cleanup. An object stuck in Terminating usually means that cleanup cannot complete, for example a controller is missing or an external resource cannot be released. It is tempting to delete the finalizer by hand. Before you do, find out which component owns it and why it is stuck, because skipping the cleanup can leave storage or cloud resources behind with nothing tracking them.

Most questions about a cluster are answered by three read-only commands, and they should come before any guessing. kubectl get lists objects, and with output set to yaml it shows the whole object, spec and status included. kubectl describe gives a human summary of one object, including the recent events about it. And kubectl get events shows what the controllers and kubelets reported, which reads best sorted by time. One caution: events are retained only for a limited time, so an empty event list does not prove nothing happened. Cleanup deserves the same care as any change. Put the context and the namespace on the command line, not in your assumptions. Delete by a label that you gave only to disposable objects, so the selector cannot reach anything that matters. And run get with exactly the same selector first, and actually read the result, because that list is precisely what delete would remove. That brings this chapter to its outcome: for any command, you can say which cluster, namespace, and objects it targets, and what will happen to their dependents, before you press enter.

A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes schedules. It is one or more containers that always run together, on the same node, and are created and removed as a unit. Inside the Pod, some things are shared. All its containers share one network namespace, so the Pod has a single IP address, and containers can talk to each other on localhost, which also means they cannot both listen on the same port. They can also share volumes, so one container can write a file that another reads. Other things stay separate. Each container has its own image and its own filesystem, runs its own process, restarts independently, and declares its own resource requests. That raises the design question: when should two containers share a Pod? Only when the helper must live and die with the main application, such as an agent shipping its logs. The catalogue API and its PostgreSQL database do not qualify. They scale differently, fail differently, and have different data lifetimes, so they belong in separate Pods, connected over the network, which is exactly how the rest of this course will build them.

Ask how a Pod is doing, and Kubernetes has three different answers. The phase is a coarse summary of the whole Pod. Pending means it was accepted but not everything is running yet, which includes waiting for a node or for an image. Running means it is bound to a node and at least one container has started. Succeeded and Failed mean all containers have ended. Second, each container has its own state: waiting, with a reason; running, since a given time; or terminated, with an exit code. Third, conditions are named checks, such as PodScheduled and Ready, each true or false with a reason. The status column that kubectl get prints blends these into one word, and that causes confusion. Running does not mean ready, and it certainly does not mean correct. CrashLoopBackOff is not a phase at all; it is the reason a container is waiting before its next restart attempt, so a Pod can sit in the Running phase while one of its containers keeps crashing. When it matters, read the status block itself, including last state, which keeps the exit code of the previous attempt.

A container cannot start until its image is on the node, and getting it there is the runtime's job, asked for by the kubelet. So the first thing that can go wrong with a new Pod is the pull. Start with how the image is named. A tag, such as version one point four, is a pointer, and someone can move it to different content later. A digest, the long sha256 value, names the exact bytes, so two nodes pulling the same digest are guaranteed to run the same thing. The pull policy decides whether the node fetches again or reuses a copy it already has. Pulls fail for a small number of reasons. The name, tag, or digest does not exist, often a typo. The registry is private, and the Pod has no pull secret granting access. Or the node cannot reach the registry at all, because of DNS, a proxy, or rate limiting. In each case the kubelet retries with growing delays, which is why the status moves from ErrImagePull to ImagePullBackOff. The useful detail is in the events: describe the Pod, and you will usually see the registry's own error message.

Each container entry in a Pod answers three questions: what to run, with which settings, and how much room to reserve for it. What to run starts with the image, named by digest. Then command and args. If you set command, it replaces the image's entrypoint; if you set args, it replaces the image's default arguments. Leave both out, and the image's own defaults apply, which is usually what you want for an image you built in the Docker course. Settings come next. Environment variables are read by the process when it starts, which matters later when we change configuration. A container port documents which port the process listens on; it is useful information, but it does not open or publish anything by itself. Finally, resources. Requests are what the scheduler reserves for this container on a node: here, one hundred millicores, a tenth of a CPU, and one hundred and twenty eight mebibytes of memory. Without requests, the scheduler is placing work blind. That is enough for now. Limits, CPU throttling, and memory-related termination are covered properly in Chapter 8.

Some work has to happen before your application starts, and some has to run beside it for as long as it lives. Kubernetes has a pattern for each. Init containers run first, one at a time, in the order you list them, and each must exit successfully before the next begins. Only when all of them have succeeded do the application containers start. If one fails, it is retried, and the Pod waits. In the catalogue example, an init container might check that the database schema exists, and another might fetch a configuration file into a shared volume for the API to read. A sidecar is a helper container that runs beside the application for the Pod's whole life, sharing its network and volumes, such as an agent that ships the API's logs. How precisely Kubernetes orders sidecar startup and shutdown has changed across versions, so check what your cluster supports rather than relying on a particular mechanism. One limit matters most. An init check passes once, at start. If the database disappears an hour later, the init container will not notice. The application must still handle that failure itself.

Kubernetes cannot see inside your process, so probes are how the application tells it about health, and each kind of probe triggers a different response. A startup probe answers, has it finished starting? Until it succeeds, the other probes are held off, which protects a slow first boot. A readiness probe answers, should this Pod receive traffic right now? When it fails, the Pod is removed from its Service's endpoints, but it is not restarted, and it rejoins when the probe passes again. A liveness probe answers, is this container stuck beyond recovery? When it fails, the container is restarted. Now match those to three situations. The catalogue API takes forty seconds to load its data on first start: that is a startup probe, not a longer liveness delay. The database goes away for a minute: readiness should fail, so traffic stops, but restarting the API would not bring the database back. The API deadlocks and will never recover: that is what liveness is for. The classic mistake is a liveness check that depends on the database, which turns one database outage into every API container restarting at once.

Pods are replaced constantly: during rollouts, when nodes are drained, when something scales down. So stopping cleanly is part of the application's job, not an edge case. Here is the sequence. When a Pod is deleted, it is marked as terminating and is removed from its Service's endpoints, so new traffic stops being routed to it. At about the same time, after any pre-stop hook runs, the main process receives a SIGTERM signal. It then has the grace period, thirty seconds unless you change it, to finish. Anything still running at the end is killed with SIGKILL, with no further chance to clean up. Two things follow for the catalogue API. It must actually handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new connections, finish the requests already in flight, and close its database connections. And because endpoint removal and the signal happen in parallel, across many components, it should keep serving for a brief moment after the signal rather than exiting instantly. Restarts are separate. The restart policy says whether a container that exits is started again, and repeated crashes are retried with growing delays.

Here is the first workload controller most applications use, and it is really two controllers stacked. You edit the Deployment. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets, and each ReplicaSet manages Pods. Each level has one job. A ReplicaSet is simple: keep exactly this many Pods matching this template, creating or deleting Pods as needed. Its Pods carry a hash label that ties them to that one ReplicaSet. The Deployment sits above, and its job is change over time. Whenever you change the Pod template, for example a new image digest, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for the new template and gradually scales the old one down. The old ReplicaSet is not deleted; it is kept at zero replicas, which is what makes a rollback possible. Changing only the replica count is different: no new template, so no new ReplicaSet, just a different number. The practical rule follows from the ownership. Always edit the Deployment. If you change a ReplicaSet or a Pod directly, its owner will overwrite or replace your change on its next reconciliation, and you will be left wondering where it went.

Let's watch reconciliation do something visible. The catalogue API's ReplicaSet wants two replicas. Delete one of its Pods, carefully, by name, in your learning namespace, and within seconds another appears. It is important to be precise about what that new Pod is. It is not the old Pod restarted or restored. The ReplicaSet simply observed one Pod where two are wanted, and created a fresh one from its template. The new Pod has a new name, a new unique ID, usually a new IP address, and possibly a different node. Anything the old container wrote to its own filesystem is gone. That has direct consequences for how you build applications. Never depend on a Pod's name or address; later chapters give you stable names through Services. Keep anything that must survive outside the container, which is what persistent storage is for in Chapter 7. And expect Pods to come and go as part of normal operation, not only during incidents. Deleting a Pod is a useful way to see replacement happen. It is not a repair, though: the new Pod runs exactly the same template, including whatever was wrong with it.

When you change the Pod template, the Deployment performs a rolling update by default: it swaps old Pods for new ones a few at a time, so the service keeps serving while it changes. Two settings shape the swap. Max surge is how many extra Pods may exist above the desired count during the change. Max unavailable is how far the number of ready Pods may drop below it. With surge one and unavailable zero, the catalogue API never has fewer than two ready Pods. And readiness is what decides when a new Pod counts, which is why the probes from Chapter 3 matter so much here. To follow progress, kubectl rollout status watches the Deployment's conditions. Now push an image that cannot be pulled. The new Pods never become ready, so the rollout stalls, and, because unavailable is zero, the old Pods keep serving. That is the design working. But be careful what complete means: every replica updated and ready. It says nothing about whether the new version returns correct answers. Rollback has a boundary too. Undo returns to the previous Pod template. It does not undo a database migration or a changed ConfigMap.

Not every workload should run forever. The catalogue import loads a batch of products and then it is finished, so it is a Job, not a Deployment. A Job runs Pods until a task completes. It counts successful completions rather than running Pods, and when a Pod fails, it starts another, up to a back-off limit. An active deadline caps the whole Job's running time, so a stuck import does not run all night. Retrying is where Jobs need real design thought. An attempt can die halfway through: the node is lost, or the Pod is evicted, after five thousand of ten thousand rows were written. The Job will retry, faithfully, and a naive import will insert those first five thousand rows a second time. Kubernetes cannot prevent that. The import has to be idempotent: safe to run more than once. Give each batch a key and skip rows already loaded under it, or load a batch inside a single transaction, so an attempt either commits completely or not at all. Finally, read the outcome carefully. A complete Job means the process exited with status zero. To know the import worked, check the data itself.

A CronJob creates a Job on a schedule, like the cron table on a Linux machine. It looks simple, but it bundles four separate questions, and it helps to answer each one deliberately. First, when. The schedule is a cron expression, so fifteen, two, star, star, star means quarter past two every day. Set the time zone explicitly rather than inheriting whatever the controller uses. Second, overlap. If last night's import is still running when tonight's is due, should both run, should tonight's be skipped, or should last night's be stopped and replaced? That is the concurrency policy: allow, forbid, or replace. For an import that writes to the same tables, forbid is usually the safe answer. Third, missed runs. The schedule is not a guaranteed timer. If the controller was unavailable at two fifteen, the run may start late, or, if too many were missed, not at all. A starting deadline bounds how late is still acceptable. Fourth, history. Each run leaves a Job behind, and limits decide how many successful and failed ones to keep, which matters because those Jobs, and their Pods' logs, are your evidence of what happened.

Some work belongs on every node, rather than on a certain number of replicas wherever there happens to be room. That is what a DaemonSet expresses. Compare the two rows on the left. A Deployment with two replicas lets the scheduler choose; two of the four nodes run the catalogue API, and the other two run nothing for it. A DaemonSet has no replica count at all. It runs one Pod on every eligible node. When a fifth node joins the cluster, it gets its agent automatically; when a node is removed, its agent goes with it. Typical DaemonSets are node agents: a log collector reading each node's log files, a metrics exporter, the cluster's own networking or storage plugins, and node-level security monitoring. You may never write one for the catalogue application, but you will meet them on every cluster. Two cautions come with them. Every node pays the agent's resource cost, so its requests multiply across the whole cluster. And node agents often need elevated privileges to read host files or configure networking, so review a DaemonSet with the care you would give infrastructure, not like an ordinary application.

With four controllers on the table, the choice comes from the shape of the work. Ask three questions. Does it run forever, or does it need to finish? Are the copies interchangeable, or does each one have its own identity? And must it run somewhere specific, such as on every node? Interchangeable, long-running copies, where any one can serve any request, are a Deployment. Work that must run to completion, possibly on a schedule, is a Job or a CronJob. One copy per node is a DaemonSet. And copies that each need a stable identity and their own storage are a StatefulSet. For the catalogue application, that gives a clear map. The API is a Deployment. The import is a Job, scheduled by a CronJob. And the PostgreSQL database is a StatefulSet, which we have deliberately not used yet. Here is the preview. A StatefulSet gives its Pods stable names, such as postgres zero, that survive replacement, and binds each one to its own persistent volume. We will build it properly alongside storage in Chapter 7. One warning now: a single database instance in a StatefulSet is stable, but it is not highly available.

The Docker course built an image for the catalogue API. A good rule from here on is: build one image and run it everywhere. Whatever differs between environments should arrive at run time, not be baked in. That separates four things that often get tangled together. The image holds the code, its dependencies, and safe defaults, and it is identical in every environment, referenced by digest. A ConfigMap holds non-secret settings for one environment: the log level, the database host, feature flags. A Secret holds credentials, such as the database password, and is handled with tighter access. And a service account gives the workload an identity of its own, which we introduce later in this chapter. Keeping these apart pays off in three ways. The image you tested is exactly the image you run, because promotion never rebuilds it. Changing a setting needs no new build. And credentials never sit inside an image layer, where anyone who can pull the image could read them. There is a simple test for any image you produce: could it run, unchanged, in both staging and production? If not, something environment-specific has leaked into it.

A ConfigMap is a named set of keys and values in a namespace, and a Pod can receive it in two ways. The first is environment variables. You can map one key to one variable, or load every key as a variable at once. The process reads them when it starts, which is simple and familiar, and works well for a handful of scalar settings like the log level or the database host. The second is files. Mount the ConfigMap as a volume, and each key becomes a file in that directory. That suits structured configuration, such as an app dot yaml with several nested settings, and it has one important property: the application can read the file again later, which matters in the next section. A few practical points. If a Pod references a ConfigMap that does not exist, its containers will not start, and the events will say why. ConfigMaps are meant for small configuration, not for data; there is a size limit, and large content belongs in a volume or a database. And reference the ConfigMap by name from the Pod template of your Deployment, so every replica receives exactly the same configuration.

A Secret is consumed much like a ConfigMap, as environment variables or files, but it marks the data as sensitive, and the system treats it a little more carefully. The first thing to understand is what it does not do. Secret values are stored base64-encoded. Base64 is an encoding that lets arbitrary bytes travel as text; it is not encryption, and anyone can decode it in a second. So anyone who can read the Secret object can read the password. Real protection comes from elsewhere. Role-based access control decides who may get or list Secrets in a namespace, and that should be very few people and workloads. Encryption at rest is a cluster setting that protects the stored data in etcd; on a managed cluster, check how your provider handles it. And plain values must stay out of Git and out of logs, which is why mounting a Secret as a file is often safer than putting it into environment variables, since environments leak into crash dumps and debugging output. Every Secret in this course uses placeholder values, like the one on screen. Chapter 9 returns to access, rotation, and who is responsible for each layer.

Here is a behaviour that surprises almost everyone the first time. You edit a ConfigMap, and the running API carries on exactly as before. Nothing is broken; what happens next depends on how the configuration was consumed. If it arrived as an environment variable, the process keeps the value it started with, until the container is restarted. If it arrived as a mounted file, the kubelet updates the file eventually, after a delay, but the application only notices if it actually reads the file again. And if the file was mounted using a subPath, it is never updated at all. Because that mix is hard to reason about, many teams take a more predictable approach: treat configuration as part of a release. Give each version of the ConfigMap a new name, or put a hash of its contents in the Pod template. Then a change to the configuration is a change to the template, and the Deployment rolls out new Pods with the new values, with the same readiness checks and rollback as an image change. The alternative to deciding this deliberately is Pods started at different times, quietly running with different configuration.

People authenticate to the cluster as users. Software running in Pods authenticates as a service account, which is a namespaced identity for a workload. Every namespace has a default service account, and Pods use it unless told otherwise. It is better to give each application its own. So the catalogue API gets a service account named catalogue-api, and its Pod template sets the service account name. Now its identity is distinct from everything else in the namespace, and permissions can be granted to it, and only it. How does the Pod prove who it is? The kubelet requests a token for that service account and mounts it into the container as a file. That token is projected: it is short-lived, it carries an audience saying which service it is meant for, and it expires. The kubelet rotates it automatically before it expires, which means client libraries must read the file again rather than caching the token forever. One important point: an identity alone grants nothing useful. A new service account can do almost nothing until roles are bound to it. That is deliberate, and Chapter 9 shows how to grant exactly what the API needs.

This chapter ends with the part Kubernetes cannot do for you. It does not start things in order. Applying the database manifest before the API manifest does not mean the database is ready first; the API may well start while PostgreSQL is still booting, and later, dependencies fail while everything is running. So the application has to cope. Consider the database disappearing for a minute. The API should retry its connection with exponential backoff and some random jitter, so a hundred replicas do not all hammer the database at the same instant when it returns. It should report itself not ready, so its Service stops sending it requests it cannot answer. Its liveness check should keep passing, because restarting the API would not bring the database back. And it should answer the requests it does receive with a clear error quickly, rather than hanging until clients time out. When the database returns, the API recovers on its own, with no restart and no manual step. At shutdown, the same care applies: finish requests and close database connections cleanly. Now the API is configured and resilient, it needs stable discovery and deliberate traffic paths, which is Chapter 6.

Kubernetes networking starts from a simple model. Every Pod gets its own IP address, and any Pod can reach any other Pod directly, even on a different node, without network address translation in between. Compare that with the Docker course, where you mapped container ports onto host ports. Here there is no mapping; a container listens on its real port at its Pod's address. Kubernetes defines this model, but it does not implement it. A network plugin, using the Container Network Interface, or CNI, assigns Pod addresses and arranges the routes between nodes. Different clusters use different plugins, and they differ in important ways, including whether they enforce the network policies we meet in Chapter 9. So record which plugin your cluster runs. The model also has a clear limit, shown at the bottom of the diagram. A Pod's address is not stable. When the ReplicaSet replaces a Pod, the new one usually has a different IP. And an address is not a name that clients can be configured with. So no client should ever hold on to a Pod IP. What clients need is a stable front for a changing set of Pods, and that is the Service.

A Service gives a changing set of Pods a stable front. It has a fixed virtual IP address and a name, and behind it, a selector chooses which Pods receive its traffic. Between the two sits the EndpointSlice. A controller keeps it up to date with the addresses of the Pods that match the selector and are ready. Traffic sent to the Service is spread across those endpoints. Look at the third Pod on the left. It matches the selector, but it is not ready, so it is not given traffic. That is readiness doing exactly what Chapter 3 promised. Ports need care. The Service's port is what clients connect to, port eighty here. The target port is the port the container actually listens on, eight thousand and eighty. If the two are mixed up, the Service exists, endpoints exist, and every connection still fails. When a Service seems to be dead, check its endpoints first, and then work through three causes. The selector matches no Pods, often a label typo. The Pods match but none is ready. Or the target port does not match the container. Each cause leaves a different piece of evidence.

Clients should find Services by name, and cluster DNS provides those names automatically. Every Service gets a DNS name built from the Service name and its namespace. From a Pod in the same namespace, the short name works: just postgres. From another namespace, you need at least the namespace too: postgres dot catalogue. The longest form, ending in svc dot cluster dot local, is fully qualified and works from anywhere in the cluster. The short form only works because each Pod's resolver searches its own namespace first, which is convenient, and also a source of confusion when the same Service name exists in two namespaces. What the lookup returns depends on the Service. A normal Service returns its single stable virtual IP. A headless Service, one with no cluster IP, returns the addresses of its ready Pods directly, which is useful when clients need to reach specific Pods, as databases in a StatefulSet sometimes do. No answer at all usually means the name, or the namespace, is wrong. For the catalogue API, set its database host to postgres dot catalogue dot svc. That is unambiguous, and it keeps working even if the API later runs in another namespace.

The type of a Service decides how far its reach extends. ClusterIP is the default, and it means inside the cluster only: a virtual IP and a DNS name reachable from Pods, but not from outside. That is exactly right for the database. NodePort builds on that, and also opens a fixed high port on every node, so anything that can reach a node can reach the Service. It exposes node addresses, and it is rarely the final answer. LoadBalancer builds on NodePort, and also asks the environment to provision an external load balancer in front of it. The key word is asks. A managed cloud cluster will usually create one, often one per Service, which costs money. A local learning cluster may have nothing to provide it, so the Service sits with its external address Pending indefinitely. Do not assume automatic infrastructure everywhere. And kubectl port-forward is not a Service type at all. It is a temporary tunnel from your own machine, through the API server, to one Pod, which ends when the command ends. It is how this course first reaches the catalogue API, and it is for learning and debugging, never for real users.

A LoadBalancer per Service gets expensive and blunt. Usually you want one entry point that routes HTTP requests to different Services by host name and path. That is what Ingress does. An Ingress object lists rules: requests for catalogue dot example, path slash products, go to the catalogue-api Service on port eighty. Here is the part that catches people. The Ingress object is only rules. Kubernetes itself does not ship anything that reads them. The work is done by an Ingress controller, a proxy you install separately, which watches Ingress objects and configures itself to match. An IngressClass names which controller is responsible for which Ingress. So consider an Ingress applied to a cluster with no controller installed. The API server accepts it, because it is a perfectly valid object. Its status simply never shows an address, and no request is ever served. A valid declaration does not imply working traffic infrastructure. Before debugging your rules, confirm that a controller exists and claims your class. Ingress is widely used and stable, and you will meet it often. Newer designs, though, increasingly use the Gateway API, which is next.

The Gateway API is the newer way to describe traffic entering a cluster, and its main idea is to split the job across objects owned by different roles. A GatewayClass describes a kind of gateway, and comes from whoever provides the infrastructure. A Gateway is an actual entry point: its listeners, ports, host names, and certificates, usually owned by the cluster operators. An HTTPRoute is owned by the application team, and it attaches to a Gateway and routes paths to Services. So the catalogue team can change its own routes without touching the shared entry point, and the operators can manage certificates without editing every application's rules. The lesson from Ingress applies here too. These are APIs, not a proxy. Something must implement them, and an implementation must be installed in your cluster. Different implementations support different features beyond the core, so record which implementation and which API version you are using, and check that a feature is supported before relying on it. When something does not route, read the status. A route reports whether its Gateway accepted it, and whether the Services it references were resolved. Those two conditions answer most questions.

Let's trace one request from a browser to the database, and mark where security changes along the way. The client connects over HTTPS to the Gateway, and that is usually where TLS terminates: the Gateway presents the certificate, which is stored in a Secret it references, and decrypts the request. From there, inside the cluster, traffic continues as plain HTTP unless you deliberately re-encrypt it, so know which hops carry clear text. The request then goes from the HTTPRoute to the Service, from the Service to one of its ready endpoints, into an API Pod, and finally the API looks up its database by name. That path is also the order to diagnose in when something fails. First, is the route accepted, with its references resolved? Second, does the Service have ready endpoints? Third, bypass everything in front: port-forward to an API Pod and see whether it answers on its own. Fourth, from the API's side, does the database name resolve, and can it connect? Each answer cuts the search in half. With the API now reachable and connected, the next chapter adds durable state, without confusing network identity with data lifetime.

Before choosing storage, ask one question: how long must this data live? Kubernetes offers several places a container can write, and they answer that question very differently. The container's own filesystem, the writable layer over its image, lives exactly as long as that container. Every restart starts fresh. An emptyDir volume lives as long as the Pod. It survives container restarts, and can be shared between the containers in the Pod, which suits scratch files and caches. But when the Pod is replaced, as Chapter 4 showed happens routinely, both are gone. ConfigMap and Secret volumes are a different category. They are projected from objects in the API, read-only by default, and they are not a place to write anything. Data that must outlive any individual Pod needs a PersistentVolumeClaim. A claim is an object of its own, separate from the Pod that uses it. When the Pod is replaced, the replacement mounts the same claim, and the data is still there. That is where PostgreSQL will keep its data directory. So the rule of thumb is simple: scratch space and caches can be ephemeral; records belong on a claim.

Persistent storage in Kubernetes is deliberately split into two objects, so that applications ask for storage without choosing a particular disk. The PersistentVolumeClaim is the application's request: I need ten gibibytes, mountable read-write by one node, from this class of storage. The PersistentVolume is an actual piece of storage known to the cluster, such as a cloud disk. When a suitable volume exists, the claim binds to it, one to one, and the Pod mounts the claim by name. Why bother with the split? Because it keeps manifests portable. The same claim works on a laptop cluster and on a cloud provider, and the platform decides what backs it. It also means the storage has a lifetime of its own, independent of the Pod, and, depending on policy, even of the claim. Reading the state is straightforward. A claim that is Pending has not found, or been given, a suitable volume yet, and a Pod using it will wait. A claim that is Bound names the volume it received. One detail of scope matters for permissions later: claims live in your namespace, but volumes are cluster-scoped objects, usually managed by the platform rather than by application teams.

In practice, almost nobody creates PersistentVolumes by hand. Instead, a claim names a StorageClass, and storage is created on demand. That is dynamic provisioning. The StorageClass is a recipe written by the platform team. Its provisioner names which storage driver handles it. Its parameters describe what kind of storage to create, such as the disk type or whether it is encrypted. Its reclaim policy says what happens to the disk when the claim is deleted, which is the next section. And its binding mode says whether to create the volume immediately, or wait until a Pod using the claim is scheduled, so the disk can be created where that Pod will run. The driver itself uses the Container Storage Interface, or CSI. It is the component that talks to the real backend, whether a cloud disk service, a storage array, or local disks, and creates, attaches, and mounts volumes. Clusters usually mark one class as the default, which a claim gets if it names none. Classes differ a lot between environments, so record which one you used. And when a claim stays Pending, the first thing to check is whether a matching class and working driver exist.

A claim carries three separate decisions, and each has its own way of failing. First, the access mode says how the volume may be attached. Read-write-once means one node at a time can mount it for writing; read-write-once-pod narrows that to a single Pod; read-write-many allows many writers at once, but only on storage backends that support it, and many do not. Second, topology. Many disks exist in one zone of a cloud region. A Pod using such a disk can only run on a node in that zone, and if none has room, the Pod stays Pending with a topology message. Waiting for the first consumer before provisioning avoids creating the disk in the wrong place. Third, reclaim. With the Delete policy, removing the claim removes the disk and its data. With Retain, the disk stays behind for someone to inspect or reuse. Many dynamic classes default to Delete, so check the policy before deleting any claim you care about. And one important non-guarantee: none of these settings makes concurrent writes safe. Two PostgreSQL servers writing to one volume will corrupt it. Consistency is the database's job, and the design keeps exactly one writer.

Now the database can be built properly. A StatefulSet is the controller for workloads whose Pods each need an identity that survives replacement. Its Pods are named by ordinal, postgres zero, postgres one, and so on, rather than with random suffixes. A volume claim template gives each Pod its own claim, so postgres zero always uses data-postgres-zero. A headless Service gives each Pod a stable DNS name. And Pods are started, stopped, and updated in order, by ordinal. Watch what happens when postgres zero is replaced, perhaps because its node failed. The replacement Pod has the same name. It reattaches the same claim, data-postgres-zero, and PostgreSQL finds its data directory exactly where it left it. Even deleting the whole StatefulSet leaves the claims in place by default, which protects the data from a careless delete. It is just as important to say what this does not provide. A StatefulSet with one replica is a single database instance. There is no replication and no automatic failover; while the Pod is being replaced, the database is down. Before concrete examples, record your assumptions: the PostgreSQL image and version, and where its data directory lives.

Three different things are often called a backup, and the differences matter on the worst day. A retained volume is just the same disk, kept. It survives a deleted claim, but it shares every failure of that disk, and it faithfully keeps every bad write, including the accidental delete you wish you could undo. A volume snapshot, taken through the storage driver, is a point-in-time copy. That is better, but it is usually only crash-consistent, as if the power had been pulled, and it often lives with the same provider as the original. An independent backup is made with the database's own tools, so it is consistent from the application's point of view, and stored somewhere that does not share the cluster's failures. The exact commands, and their consistency guarantees, come from PostgreSQL's documentation, not from Kubernetes. And whichever you use, a backup is only proven by restoring it. Restore into an isolated target, never over the live database. Compare record counts with what you expect. Run representative catalogue API queries against the restored data. And record how long the whole process took, because that number is your real recovery time.

Running the database inside the cluster, as this chapter has done, is a choice rather than a default, and it is worth weighing against the alternative. In the cluster, you own everything. You run the backups and test the restores, you perform PostgreSQL upgrades and tuning, and if you want replication and automatic failover, you build and operate them, typically with a specialised operator. In return, the database sits close to the application and on the same bill. A managed database service, run by a cloud provider, moves a lot of that work. The provider operates failover, patching, and scheduled backups. But it does not move all of it. You still own who can connect, the network rules, and the cost, and you still need to prove that a restore actually works. The encouraging part is that the catalogue API does not need to care. Either way, it sees a DNS name and a Secret containing credentials. Switching from one to the other changes configuration, not the image, which is the payoff of Chapter 5. Storage has one more consequence we have only touched on: where data lives constrains where Pods can run. That connects us to scheduling and capacity, in Chapter 8.

Chapter 3 introduced requests as what the scheduler reserves. Now we need the full picture, because requests and limits do different jobs, and CPU and memory behave differently when they run short. Requests decide placement. The scheduler adds up the requests of everything on a node and only places a Pod where its requests fit. Limits are enforced while the container runs. Units first. CPU is measured in cores, or thousandths of a core, so five hundred m is half a core. Memory is measured in bytes, and the suffixes Mi and Gi are powers of two. Now the difference that matters. A container that tries to use more CPU than its limit is throttled. It is simply given less CPU time, so it slows down, and you see it as rising latency, not as an error. A container that uses more memory than its limit is killed by the kernel, reported as OOMKilled, exit code one hundred thirty seven, and then restarted. There is no slow fallback for memory. So size memory limits for the peak, not the average. A practical start: set requests near measured use, set a memory limit, and think carefully before adding a CPU limit.

The scheduler places Pods by accounting, not by how busy nodes look right now, and that surprises people the first time. Each node offers an allocatable amount of CPU and memory to Pods, which is its capacity minus what the system reserves for itself. The scheduler subtracts the sum of the requests of every Pod already placed there. A new Pod fits only if its own requests fit in what remains. Look at the table. A new catalogue API replica requests five hundred millicores. Node one has only two hundred left to request, and node three has fifty, even though both are nearly idle by measured use. Node two is actually the busiest by measured use, yet it is the only node with eight hundred millicores still unrequested, so that is where the replica goes. If no node had room, the Pod would stay Pending. When you see a Pending Pod, describe it. A FailedScheduling event says how many nodes were considered, and why each was rejected: insufficient CPU, insufficient memory, or a constraint it could not satisfy. The fix is in the requests, the cluster's capacity, or the constraints, never in deleting and recreating the Pod.

Requests decide whether a Pod fits. A second set of tools decides where it is allowed to go, and they come in two directions. In one direction, a Pod chooses nodes. The simplest is a node selector: the node must carry these exact labels. Required node affinity expresses richer rules, such as a zone in a list, but it is still mandatory; if no node satisfies it, the Pod stays Pending. Preferred affinity is a weighted preference. It scores the candidate nodes, but if none matches, the Pod is placed anyway. That makes preferences the safer default. In the other direction, a node refuses Pods. A taint on a node keeps Pods off it, for example to reserve nodes with special hardware. A toleration on a Pod lets it onto a tainted node anyway. Here is the subtle part: a toleration only permits placement. It does not demand it. A Pod that tolerates the GPU taint may still land on an ordinary node. If you want Pods both allowed onto, and kept on, particular nodes, pair a toleration with affinity. And when Pods are Pending, check for a required rule that no node can satisfy.

Running two replicas of the catalogue API only helps if they fail separately, and placement decides whether they do. A failure domain is anything that can fail as a unit: a node, a whole availability zone, occasionally a region. Nodes carry labels naming their zone and host, and the scheduler can use them. Look at the top band. Both replicas landed in zone a, perhaps simply because it had the most free capacity. When zone a has an outage, both are lost together, and having two was worth nothing. Topology spread constraints prevent that. They tell the scheduler to keep replicas balanced across a topology key, such as zone, with a maximum skew: with a skew of one, no zone may have more than one replica more than any other. The constraint can be hard, refusing to schedule rather than break it, or soft, preferring balance but placing anyway. Spread does not fix everything, which is the bottom band. The surviving replicas must have capacity to carry the whole load. The single database still lives in one zone, so it remains the real limit. And spread is evaluated at placement time; the scheduler does not move running Pods later.

On a shared cluster, each namespace usually gets a budget, and two objects enforce it. Both change what your manifests actually request, which is why they belong in this chapter. A ResourceQuota caps the namespace's totals: the sum of CPU and memory requests and limits, and counts of objects such as Pods. When creating a Pod would exceed the quota, the API refuses it. And once a quota covers requests, every Pod must declare them, or it is refused too. A LimitRange works per container. It can fill in default requests and limits for containers that do not set them, and it rejects containers whose values fall outside its minimum and maximum. The practical effect is that the object stored in the cluster may differ from the one you applied, because defaults were filled in on the way. Read it back with output yaml to see what was really requested. One failure mode is easy to miss. When a quota is full, it is the ReplicaSet's attempt to create a Pod that is refused, so the Deployment looks fine while its replica count never rises. The evidence is in the ReplicaSet's events.

The HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjusts a Deployment's replica count based on metrics. It is a chain of dependencies, and every link has to work. Demand rises. A metrics pipeline reports the new usage; for CPU, that is usually the metrics server add-on, which not every cluster has. The autoscaler compares usage with its target, for example sixty percent of the CPU request, and computes a desired replica count in proportion. Then the Deployment creates Pods and the scheduler has to place them. Now walk through the failures. If no metrics API is installed, the autoscaler has nothing to act on and says so in its status. If the containers have no CPU requests, utilisation, which is usage divided by request, is undefined. If the cluster has no free capacity, the new replicas sit Pending, unless node autoscaling, in the next section, adds room. And the hardest case: if the real bottleneck is the single database, more API replicas only add more connections to an overloaded database. Two practical rules. The autoscaler owns the replica field, so remove replicas from your own manifest, as Chapter 2's field ownership warned. And set the minimum and maximum deliberately.

Horizontal autoscaling changes the number of replicas. Two other kinds of autoscaling change different numbers, and this course only orients you to them. Vertical autoscaling changes requests. It watches what containers actually use and recommends, or applies, better request values. It is an add-on rather than built in, and applying new values may recreate Pods. Do not let it and a horizontal autoscaler both react to the same CPU signal, or they will fight each other. Node autoscaling changes the number of nodes. It is provided by your cloud or an add-on, and it reacts to Pods that are Pending because no node has capacity, by adding a node. It also removes underused nodes, which means evicting the Pods on them, so the disruption rules of Chapter 12 matter. And it takes minutes, not seconds, because machines have to boot. None of this is free. Spare headroom costs money; no headroom costs latency during a spike. Reacting quickly causes flapping up and down; reacting slowly falls behind. Always set bounds. Finally, shared capacity and placement create authority boundaries, who may use what, and those need explicit security controls, which is Chapter 9.

Security in Kubernetes starts at the API server, and every request to it, from a person with kubectl or from a Pod using its token, passes three gates in order. The first is authentication: who are you? The server checks a certificate, a token, or a login from an identity provider. If it cannot establish an identity, the answer is four hundred and one, unauthorised. The second is authorisation: may this identity perform this action on this resource? In most clusters that is role-based access control, the subject of section three. If not, the answer is four hundred and three, forbidden. The third is admission. Admission controllers can adjust an incoming object, for example filling in defaults, and then validate it, and reject it if it breaks a policy, such as the Pod security rules in section four. Only after all three is the object stored. Reading the refusal tells you which gate failed. Forbidden means your identity was fine and the permission was missing. An admission denial names the policy. And one thing is drawn apart on purpose: the API Pod's connection to the database is ordinary network traffic, and none of these gates applies to it. Controlling that is the job of network policy.

People and software reach the API in different ways, but the goal for both is the same: an identity that belongs to exactly one person or one workload, with credentials that expire. Start with people. Kubernetes has no user object; you cannot create a user with kubectl. Human identities come from outside, most often from an identity provider your organisation already uses, sometimes from client certificates. The provider also asserts which groups a person belongs to, and groups are usually the best thing to bind roles to, because joining a team then grants the right access, and leaving it removes it. Workloads use service accounts, which are ordinary objects in a namespace. Chapter 5 gave the catalogue API its own account; the import Job gets another, so each can be granted exactly what it needs and nothing the other needs. Their tokens are projected and expire. Then the habits to stop. One admin kubeconfig shared across a team, so no action can be traced to a person. Permissions granted to the default service account, which every Pod in the namespace uses unless told otherwise. And long-lived static tokens, anywhere, that keep working long after they leak.

Role-based access control decides what an authenticated identity may do. The first thing to know is that it is purely additive: there are no deny rules, and nothing is allowed until some binding grants it. That makes least privilege the natural design. It uses four objects. A Role is a set of permissions within one namespace. A ClusterRole is a set of permissions that can apply cluster-wide, or be reused in many namespaces. A binding attaches a role to subjects: users, groups, or service accounts. A RoleBinding grants it inside one namespace; a ClusterRoleBinding grants it everywhere, so treat those with real care. Each rule names API groups, resources, verbs, and optionally specific resource names. Watch one trap: listing or watching Secrets returns their values, not just their names. The example on screen grants the import Job's service account permission to get one named ConfigMap in the catalogue namespace, and nothing else. Contrast that with binding cluster-admin, which grants everything, everywhere. When a workload gets a forbidden error, the fix is to add the one missing permission. You can test any permission first, impersonating the service account with kubectl auth can-i.

Access control limits what an identity can ask the API for. A security context limits what a container can actually do once it is running, which matters if the application is ever compromised. The container on screen is locked down. It refuses to run as root. It cannot gain more privileges than it started with. It drops every Linux capability. Its root filesystem is read-only, so anything it writes must go to a declared volume. And it uses the runtime's default seccomp profile, which blocks unusual system calls. Most applications, including the catalogue API, run perfectly well like this. To make such settings a rule rather than a hope, Kubernetes defines Pod Security Standards at three levels: privileged, which allows anything; baseline, which blocks known escalations; and restricted, which requires hardening like this. Pod Security Admission applies a level to a namespace in three modes. Enforce rejects violating Pods. Audit records violations, and warn shows them to the person applying. A sensible path is warn first, fix what it reports, then enforce. One surprise is common: the Deployment is admitted, but the Pods it tries to create are refused, and the evidence is in the ReplicaSet's events.

By default, the Pod network is flat: every Pod can reach every other Pod in the cluster. Network policy narrows that down to the paths the application actually needs. Policies select Pods by label, and once a Pod is selected by any policy for a direction, ingress or egress, it becomes isolated in that direction: only traffic some policy allows gets through. Like RBAC, the rules are additive. So the usual pattern is a default-deny policy for the namespace, then a small set of explicit allows. For the catalogue application, that is three paths. The Gateway may reach the API on port eight thousand and eighty. The API and the import Job may reach the database on port five four three two. And everything needs egress to cluster DNS on port fifty three, over UDP and TCP. That last rule is the one everyone forgets, and the symptom is confusing: nothing can resolve a name, so everything fails, even the allowed paths. Then the crucial caveat. Policies are enforced by the network plugin, not by Kubernetes itself. A plugin without policy support accepts the objects and silently ignores them. So test it: confirm that a blocked path really is blocked, not only that allowed paths work.

Chapter 5 said a Secret's base64 encoding is not protection. Here are the layers that are, and the point to take from them is that each layer has to be owned by someone. First, access. Get, list, and watch on Secrets all reveal the values. And there is an indirect path: anyone allowed to create Pods in a namespace can create a Pod that mounts any Secret there, and read it. So review who can create workloads, not only who can read Secrets. Second, rotation. The safe order is to create the new credential, roll out the Pods that use it so they pick it up, and only then revoke the old one, because revoking first takes the application down. Practise this before an incident forces you to do it in a hurry. Third, encryption at rest. Whether Secret data is encrypted inside etcd is a control-plane setting, often backed by a key management service. On a managed cluster, find out what the provider does. And remember that backups of cluster state contain Secrets too. Fourth, responsibility. Platform teams usually own encryption and audit; application teams own the values and their rotation. Write that down, because a layer nobody owns is a layer nobody maintains.

Two questions finish the security chapter: what exactly is running, and who else shares the cluster with it? For the first, a digest fixes which bytes run, which Chapter 3 introduced. But a digest only proves identity, not safety. A trusted registry, and where available, image signatures, tell you where those bytes came from. Scanning tells you which known vulnerabilities they contain, and since new flaws are published constantly, images that were clean last month need scanning again. Admission policies can require these properties, for example rejecting any image not pulled from your registry. For the second question, the usual unit of tenancy is the namespace: one per team or application, each with its own access rules, quotas, and network policies. That is a reasonable boundary between cooperating teams. It is not strong isolation. Nodes, the kernel, and the control plane are still shared, so tenants who must not trust each other at all belong in separate clusters. And that leads to the theme of the whole chapter: base64, a namespace, or an image digest is each one layer, never sufficient on its own. With these controls reviewed, they now have to survive repeatable releases and changes of ownership, which is Chapter 10.

A release you can repeat has exactly two inputs, and you should be able to name both precisely. One is the set of manifests in source control. The other is the image digest. The image is built once, by continuous integration, from one commit, and the pipeline records the digest the registry returned. From then on, that digest is what moves. Staging runs it and is tested against it. Production runs the same digest, so the bytes that passed the tests are the bytes that serve users. That is promotion. Two common shortcuts break it. A moving tag such as latest can be pointed at different content between your test and your deploy, so you no longer know what is running. And rebuilding the image separately for each environment produces new bytes that were never tested, even from the same commit. Manifests get the same discipline. They live in source control, reviewed like code, with history and authorship. The cluster then holds a copy of that record, not the record itself. Which means anything changed only in the cluster, by hand, is undocumented, and will be lost or fought over later, as the last section of this chapter shows.

Most of what differs between staging and production is small: a replica count, some resource sizes, the image digest being promoted. Copying whole manifest folders per environment quickly lets them drift apart. Kustomize keeps one base and a small overlay per environment. The base holds what every environment shares: the catalogue API's Deployment, its Service, its ConfigMap, and a kustomization file listing them. Each overlay refers to the base and patches only what differs, for example two replicas in staging and three in production, both pinned to the same digest. One feature connects nicely to Chapter 5. A ConfigMap generator appends a hash of the content to the ConfigMap's name. Change a value, and the name changes, so the Pod template changes, and the Deployment rolls out new Pods with the new configuration, with readiness checks and rollback. That is the predictable alternative to editing ConfigMaps in place. The working habit is to render first. kubectl kustomize with an overlay prints the final objects, and those rendered objects, not the base and patches, are what you read and diff before applying. Kustomize is built into kubectl, and there is no template language to learn.

You will often install software you did not write, such as an ingress controller or a monitoring agent, and much of it is distributed with Helm. This course only orients you to it. Helm has three nouns. A chart is a versioned package: a set of templates that produce manifests, plus default values. Values are your settings for one particular installation, overriding the defaults, kept in a file per environment in source control. A release is one installation of a chart in a cluster, with a name, and every install, upgrade, or rollback creates a new numbered revision, whose history Helm stores in the cluster itself. A few habits keep it safe. Render the chart with helm template and read what it will actually apply, because templates can produce far more than their values suggest. Pin the chart version as carefully as an image digest, since an upgrade can change many objects at once. For a third-party chart, know who maintains it and how quickly they fix problems. And remember the lesson of section five: rolling back a release restores the previous rendered manifests. It does not roll back data or a database migration.

Chapter 4 showed a rollout stalling on a bad image. A correct release can stall too, for a reason that has nothing to do with the code: the cluster has no room. With max surge one, the Deployment wants to create one extra Pod before removing an old one, and that extra Pod needs capacity, which Chapter 8 showed is a matter of requests. If no node has room, the surge Pod stays Pending. With max unavailable zero, the old Pods are kept and keep serving, so users see nothing wrong, but the release never completes. After the progress deadline, the Deployment's Progressing condition turns false, with a reason. That is the design working safely, provided the settings are deliberate. So learn to read the evidence in layers. Rollout status follows the Deployment and eventually reports the timeout. The conditions say why. The ReplicaSet counts show how far the rollout got: how many new Pods exist and how many are ready. And then the real test, which Kubernetes cannot do for you: the application's own error rates and latency during and after the change. Promote a release to the next environment only when all of these agree.

Rollback sounds like an undo button for a release. In Kubernetes, it is narrower than that, and the gap is where outages hide. kubectl rollout undo returns the Deployment to the previous ReplicaSet's Pod template, which includes the previous image. That is all. ConfigMaps or Secrets that were edited in place stay as they are. A database migration that the new version ran has already changed the schema. And any rows the new version wrote since are still there, in whatever shape it wrote them. So rollback is only safe if the old code can live with what the new code left behind, and that has to be designed in advance. The usual technique is expand, then contract. First expand: add the new column or table in a way the old code simply ignores. Release code that works with both the old and the new shape. Only later, once you are sure you will not roll back, contract: remove what the old code needed. Now the incompatible case. Suppose a migration drops a column the old code still reads. Rolling back the image then starts old code against a schema it cannot use, and makes the outage worse rather than better.

Once manifests and digests live in source control, something has to get them into the cluster, and there are two broad models. Both start from a reviewed, merged change. They differ in who applies it, how often, and from where. In CI delivery, the pipeline that ran the tests also applies the manifests to the cluster. It is simple and familiar. But the pipeline needs credentials that can change the cluster, stored outside it, and it applies once and then finishes. If someone later changes the cluster by hand, nothing notices. In the GitOps model, an agent running inside the cluster pulls the desired state from the repository and applies it. No cluster credentials need to exist outside the cluster. And the agent does not stop: it keeps comparing the cluster with the repository, and reports drift or reverts it. If that sounds familiar, it should. It is the reconciliation loop from Chapter 1, applied to delivery itself. The two are not exclusive. CI typically still builds, tests, and records the digest, and then updates the repository, and the GitOps agent deploys from there. Either way, every change begins as a reviewed commit, not as a command typed at a cluster.

Drift is the cluster differing from the record in source control. Some drift is just untidy. The dangerous kind is two writers fighting over the same field, and the replica count is the classic example. The manifest in Git says three replicas. The autoscaler from Chapter 8, under load, wants five. And during an incident, someone ran kubectl scale and set four. Now add a GitOps agent that faithfully resets the field to three, as it was told to. The autoscaler raises it again, the agent resets it, and the replica count flaps, creating and deleting Pods exactly when the system is under the most load. Every writer is doing its job correctly; the design is what is wrong. The fix is a single owner per field. If the autoscaler owns replicas, remove replicas from the manifest in Git entirely, so the agent has no opinion about it. Field managers, from Chapter 2, show which writer last set each field, which turns a mystery into evidence. And when an emergency demands a hand edit, put the change back into Git immediately, so the record and the cluster agree again. That ownership and release evidence is also what the next chapter, on diagnosis, relies on.

Every diagnosis in this chapter starts from evidence, and Kubernetes keeps three kinds of it, each for a different length of time. Status is the current truth: an object's conditions, its containers' states, their exit codes and restart counts. It is overwritten as things change, so it tells you what is true now, not what happened. Events are what the components reported: the scheduler failing to place a Pod, the kubelet pulling an image, a probe failing. They are very useful, and they are kept only for a short time, often around an hour, and then they are gone. Container logs are what the application itself wrote to standard output and error. The previous flag shows the logs of the container that crashed, rather than its fresh replacement, which is usually what you need. Logs are rotated on the node, and deleted with the Pod. That leads to the most important habit: treat an absence as weak evidence. No event may simply mean it expired. An empty log may mean the process crashed before writing anything. A single exit code has many possible causes. Confirm each hypothesis from a second source, and ship logs off the node if you will need them later.

Logs tell you what happened to individual requests. Metrics tell you how much, how often, and since when, which is usually the first thing you need in an incident. Four signals, read together, describe most service problems. Latency, measured as a high percentile such as the ninety-fifth, because an average hides the slow requests users actually notice. Errors, as a rate of failed responses. Traffic, how much demand there is. And saturation, how close a resource is to its limit: CPU throttling, a full database connection pool. Now read the illustrative graph on the left. The catalogue API's ninety-fifth percentile latency sat around one hundred and twenty milliseconds, then stepped up to nearly four hundred, exactly at the release marker. A step at a release points strongly at the change itself. A slow climb would suggest something else: rising load, a memory leak, or growing data. Then compare with traffic. If traffic is unchanged and answers are slower, the cause is inside the system. Metrics come from two places: the application exposes its own, and the cluster adds resource usage. This course names no particular monitoring product, because the signals matter more than the tool.

A latency metric tells you requests got slower. It does not tell you where the time went. For that, you follow one request through the system. The simplest version is a request ID. The Gateway assigns an identifier to each incoming request, every component passes it along on its outgoing calls, and every log line about that request includes it. Then a single search for one ID joins the Gateway, API, and database logs into a single story. That alone is worth doing on the first day. Tracing goes a step further. Each hop records a span: what it did, when it started, and how long it took. Spans nest, so the API handler's span contains the database query's span. Look at the example.
